slides.title: Functions
slides.say: Welcome. This chapter is about functions: how to define one, what goes in and out, where the names live, and what happens when something goes wrong. Every code slide shows the code, a plain explanation, and the result as a table, chart or drawing.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Four parts: defining and calling, the call stack and scope, handling errors, and short programs. Each code slide has its place in the chapter-code tab of the page, in this same order.

slides.title: Two questions this chapter answers
slides.say: Two questions to carry through the chapter. What does a call do with its arguments and its result? And which names does a function see, and what happens when it fails?

slides.title: Part 1: Defining and calling
slides.say: Part one. A function is written once with def and used many times. Watch what goes in as arguments and what comes out as a return value, and what a missing return gives back.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: defining a function
slides.say: A recipe card is written once and cooked many times. That is a function. A black box is a vending machine: you press buttons and never see the machinery. Ask students for an everyday black box.

slides.title: def defines a function; a call runs it
slides.say: Def only stores the function. Each call runs the body once with its own value for name. Run it on the page, then add a third call.

slides.title: Deduplication: a function replaces copied code
slides.say: The pasted copy has a stray space and nobody sees it. The function holds the text once. This is deduplication: fix a thing in one place.

slides.title: Story: the function is invented in Cambridge
slides.say: David Wheeler, with Wilkes and Gill, is credited with the closed subroutine around 1951. The jump to a subroutine was called the Wheeler jump. Ask students: what must a call remember so it can return?

slides.title: Everyday pictures: values in, values out
slides.say: Parameters are blank lines on the order form; arguments fill them. Return is the plate leaving the kitchen. None is the empty tray: the call finished, but nothing came back.

slides.title: Arguments fill the parameters, in order
slides.say: Parameters are the names in the def line; arguments are the values in the call. Matching is by position, so swapping the arguments swaps the meaning.

slides.title: return hands a value back to the caller
slides.say: Return ends the call and hands a value back. The call expression is replaced by that value. Calls nest: the inner call runs first.

slides.title: None: what a function gives back without return
slides.say: A function without return gives back None. Shout printed but returned nothing. Len is different: it returns a number. Predict before the run.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: named options and built-ins
slides.say: Named parameters are switches with labels, so order does not matter. Print speaks, input listens, len measures. Ask students which of the three hands a value back.

slides.title: Named parameters: sep and end of print()
slides.say: Sep sets the separator and end sets what comes after the last value. Both are named parameters of print. The table shows the invisible characters.

slides.title: Default values and keyword-only parameters
slides.say: A default makes an argument optional. The star makes the parameters after it keyword-only, so they must be named in the call.

slides.title: A default value is made once: the shared list
slides.say: The default list is made once, when def runs. Calls without bag share it. The safe habit is a default of None and a fresh list inside the body.

slides.title: Part 2: The call stack and scope
slides.say: Part two. Every active call has a frame on the call stack. Names are looked up by scope rules: local first, then global. The global statement is the one exception.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: the call stack
slides.say: Each call puts one sticky note on the pile. The top note is the running call. When it returns, the note is removed and the one below continues.

slides.title: The call stack: one frame for every active call
slides.say: Inspect.stack lists the waiting frames. Subtract the base and you get the depth of each call. The drawing and the chart show the stack growing to three and shrinking back to zero.

slides.title: A frame object knows its function and its caller
slides.say: A frame object belongs to one running call. It knows its code and its caller. Inner sees outer as its caller.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: scope
slides.say: A local variable is a notepad in one room. The global variable is the notice board in the hall. Rooms read the hall but never each other's notepads. Global is the written permission to write on the board.

slides.title: A local variable lives only during its call
slides.say: Eggs exists only while make runs. After the return it is gone, so the lookup outside fails with a NameError.

slides.title: Local scopes are walled off; globals can be read
slides.say: A function may read a global name. It may not read another function's local name. The green arrow is allowed, the red one is blocked.

slides.title: The same name can be three different variables
slides.say: Three scopes can each hold a name spam. They are three different variables. The table shows where each one lives.

slides.title: The global statement reaches the global variable
slides.say: Without the global statement, an assignment creates a local variable. With it, the assignment changes the global one. Compare the two values after each call.

slides.title: nonlocal: the middle case between local and global
slides.say: Nonlocal is the middle case: the name belongs to the enclosing function, not to the module. Each call of tick changes the same count. Python 3 added nonlocal; the book does not cover it.

slides.title: Scope identification: does the body read or assign?
slides.say: Python scans the whole body. A name that is assigned is local, unless declared global. A name that is only read is global.

slides.title: Assign later, crash earlier: UnboundLocalError
slides.say: The body assigns eggs, so eggs is local everywhere in the function, also before the assignment. Reading it first raises UnboundLocalError, a kind of NameError.

slides.title: Part 3: Handling errors
slides.say: Part three. An error is an exception. Try marks the risky code; except says what to do. Where you put the try decides which statements still run.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: errors
slides.say: Try is the act, except is the net. The traceback is the incident report. Ask students what a program should do when the net catches a fall.

slides.title: try and except recover from an error
slides.say: Try runs the risky code. If ZeroDivisionError is raised, except returns a message instead. The program goes on with the next call.

slides.title: Where the try goes (1): inside the loop
slides.say: Try inside the loop handles each call on its own. The failed call is reported and the loop carries on with the next value.

slides.title: Where the try goes (2): around all the calls
slides.say: Try around all calls: the first error jumps to except and the remaining calls are skipped. The chart counts what completed.

slides.title: One except for several kinds of error
slides.say: A tuple of types catches several kinds. As err gives the exception object. Python 3.14 allows the list without parentheses; older versions do not.

slides.title: A traceback lists the calls that led to the error
slides.say: The traceback is the stack of calls saved when the exception was raised. Extract tb lists them, oldest first. The drawing follows the path.

slides.title: Story: except loses its parentheses in Python 3.14
slides.say: PEP 758 was resolved on 14 March 2025 and ships in Python 3.14. Older versions reject the bare list, so the slides keep the parentheses. Ask students which Python version they run.

slides.title: Part 4: Short programs
slides.say: Part four. Two animation programs from the book, written to run without waiting, and one practice program, the Collatz sequence. Predict each result before the run.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: short programs
slides.say: Zigzag swings like a pendulum. Spike climbs and descends by squares. Both are small programs that combine loops, lists and functions.

slides.title: Short program: Zigzag
slides.say: The band moves one place per step and turns at the edges. The chart shows the indent of each step: up to 20 and back down.

slides.title: Short program: Spike
slides.say: The lines grow as squares and shrink again. The chart shows the lengths. Multiply a string by a number to get a line of that length.

slides.title: Practice program: the Collatz sequence
slides.say: One function is one step of the rule. A loop repeats it until the number reaches 1. The chart shows the path of 6.

slides.title: Story: an unsolved problem fits in a small function
slides.say: Lothar Collatz introduced his rule in 1937. Paul Erdős said mathematics may not be ready for such problems. The collatz function on the slide is the whole rule. Ask: why can a computer check but not prove?

slides.title: Current Python adds more
slides.say: Python moves on. One printed error message of the book has changed wording. Python 3.14 defers annotations and allows except without parentheses. Nonlocal is the middle case between local and global.

slides.title: Summary
slides.say: Five sentences to keep. The chart counts the code examples of each part.

slides.title: Practice Questions
slides.say: Four drills. Predict first, then run on the page. Ask students to explain each answer in one sentence.

slides.title: Resources: where to go next
slides.say: Start with the book chapter and the Python tutorial. The stories link to first-hand sources. Choose one link and read it before the next class.
